utterances.text: The chief of engineering that is an expert for the brigade, if the commander signs an order, the chief of engineering may relay that order to the commander of the engineer company. He can suggest tasks to help implement and fill these orders, but he doesn't himself write orders to the commander. The commander writes the orders, doesn't he, the daily orders?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a very complex procedure. Usually, it is neither the commander of the brigade nor the commander of the company who actually write those orders. It is officers below them who do that. And the higher commanders sign them in order to authenticate them, to give them proper authority. I've already explained that if the chief of engineers has no other duties but to be the chief of engineers, he is an advisory body, so to say, to the commander of the engineers. And thus, he does not have the right to be in command of the commander of the engineers. That's one case scenario. The second case scenario, I don't know what you're implying in your question, the second possibility is that for certain reasons, the commander estimates that the -- that Jevtic, whom we mentioned a little while ago, was a layperson, in military terms. And then he issues an order that the engineers company will be commanded by the chief of engineers. That is the prerogative of the commander which he can use. Our commander, Pandurevic, used this prerogative of his, and at such moments if the commander issues an order to the chief, for example, the chief of engineers in this specific case, to monitor the work and command the engineers company, in that case, the chief of engineers is de facto the superior officer to the commander of the engineers. And this is a decision that can be made, and this happened in practice, in everyday life.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: If this were to take place, if the commander took the authority away from the commander of the engineering company and transferred to the chief of engineering, it would have to be a written order, a written disposition, reflecting that change of command, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be either a written order or a verbal order. They have the same effect. And according to rules, a commander has the right to use either/or. The commander can define this for a specific task. For example, we are building a bridge, and the commander can say that the chief of engineers will be in charge of the command of that. Or he can appoint the chief of engineers to be in charge for a certain period of time. For example, for a certain number of days or months.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: But that is an exception to the procedure as its written in the exhibit that we've used on the rules of utilisation of the engineering company. That's an exception. That's not the normal procedure.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right, that is an exception to the rules that we have quoted a while ago. But we did not have enough officers at the time, and Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic believed that Jevtic and Bogicevic had not completed military education, so he believed that they had to have somebody with qualifications, and that's why he made such a decision. And this did not only apply to engineers; this applied to communications and to some other units that we had at the time for that reason.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: You were deputy commander on the 13th, 14th, and 15th of July, 1995. You didn't issue any order that took the command of the engineering company away from Dragan Jevtic, did you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. There was a prior order issued by the commander which was in effect throughout the war. And this order regulated this issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And that order was that Jokic was chief of engineering; Dragan Jevtic was commander of engineering, and Slavko Bogicevic would be the deputy commander of engineering. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And in addition to that, Jokic controlled the engineers company in practical terms when it came to the professional part of their duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: When you say "he controlled," he recommended and -- not initiated but implemented orders from the commander. Is that right, which is part of the description?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the commander who issued orders. It would be either Pandurevic or myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Okay. I have another document to introduce at this time. It is - I'm sorry - D13/3. The Zvornik Brigade engineering company daily orders logbook.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Do you see that, D13/3?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Mr. Obrenovic, have you had a moment to review this? Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And it's a duty officer of the engineering company logbook -- I mean, a logbook for the engineering company?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a copy of the daily orders of the commander of the engineers company.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you. And I just want to bring to your attention, each one of these days has a duty officer at the company command. Just for the Trial Chamber's information, there is a duty officer in each company, too, which is different from the operational duty officer at command headquarters. Isn't there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And there is also a duty officer that sits at the entrance gate, the kiosk, when you come into the command, isn't there? Isn't he called the duty officer also?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he isn't. He is a soldier on duty at the reception. It depends largely on how things are regulated.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I just want to ask you, say, on July 13th, the company commander, Mr. Jevtic, signs that the engineering company had engaged in normal engineering operations. They do lay mines, don't they? That's one of their duties?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 13th?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: This is the 13th.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are five tasks here for the 13th. And the task that you have mentioned is also there. And a group of 15 soldiers are mentioned who set an ambush on the orders of the brigade command. This is not an engineering task. This is the last line under item 6.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And this is when you put together the remnant company to go help defend at the front line which consisted of engineering company, combat people, and you just took from every area that you could put together a remnant company to defend. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The basic purpose of engineers is not to participate in combat but to provide for the various logistics tasks, engineering tasks for the life of units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me one second. Just to try to clarify, the translation says in task 6 "75 conscripts." Mr. Obrenovic said 15. It might be a good idea to see which is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, altogether, there are six tasks on that day. But the witness said there are only five.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I can clear that up, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Mr. Obrenovic, when you said 75 conscripts, did you mean all 75 came from the engineering unit, or just a portion of them came from the engineering unit to be a part of the conscripts. Or is that number wrong?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember having said 75. It says 15, 15 soldiers of the engineers company. The handwriting is very unclear. But certainly, there were 15 of them. Whatever it says here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And can we go on to the 14th of July. The duty officer at the engineering company command was Vojislav Sekanic, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's when it says, second line.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And we know that Dragan Jevtic, the commander, was not present. So can we assume that Bogicevic was acting commander as deputy commander that day in the engineering company?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it was supposed to be.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And then on the 15th, we have the duty officer as Sergeant Damjan Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And the deputy commander on that day would have still been Mr. Bogicevic, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, unless he was somewhere else, but he was supposed to be.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And on the 16th, we have Marko Kljestan as duty officer, but because Mr. Jevtic was still absent, Mr. Bogicevic was the deputy commander. Right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it was supposed to be.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And every one of these documents are confirmed and signed by the company commander Dragan Jevtic. Right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it reads: "Dragan Jevtic." Then there's a signature underneath the name. It's probably Jevtic's signature, but not that I can actually remember what his signature looked like. This may be his signature, but he was certainly at Snagovo, and he may have signed this later upon his return. I'm not familiar with the details.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes. Did you know that he backdated these and signed these documents when he returned from the front?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was not exactly keeping track of these things then, at that time. I was not really paying attention to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: But for the record, there is no signature of Dragan Jokic on any of these engineering company logbook pages, are there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It appears not. Major Jokic's signature cannot be found on any of these documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I'm trying to figure out what this exhibit is. One second. Your Honour, the next document that we'll be dealing with will be D11/3. And it is the "Responsibility of the Duty Officer, Manual for the Work of Commands and Staffs." We're going to leave the engineering company now and go to the duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Have you had time to look at this document, Mr. Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've had a look briefly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Okay. You were asked by the Prosecution to describe the duties of the duty officer, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And do you think that your answer conforms with the manual on the work of command and staffs, paragraph 65?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly can't claim that I was able to quote the exact duties of the operations duty officer. I listed them by rote to the best of my recollection at that moment. Certainly, what you should do in that situation is go back to the rules and simply read them. I never claimed that I knew all of the duties pertaining to the operations duty officer by heart, and that I could just recite them off the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to go through and see if you confirm the written rules concerning the duty officer. And we're talking about the operations duty officer, because on the next pages there are descriptions of other duty officers. But the one we're concerned with is the operations duty officer. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The exact reference to what we had in the brigade would be the operations duty officer of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And the duty operations officer always has an assistant when he's operating on his 24-hour shift, doesn't he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And I believe you confirmed that the assistant takes over somewhere between midnight and 6.00 in the morning. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And the operational duty at the command post, it's organised by the chief of staff, isn't it? Or is that just the chief of staff at the logistics command post?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we have -- we -- there are two things. One thing is the operations duty officer, and the other thing is the operations duty for operative issues, which is carried out by the operations duty team. And then one of the officers is appointed. These are simply two different procedures.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: The duty shift is served in the duty officer's operations rooms, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The duty officer is on duty in the office, the office we pointed out, both yesterday and this morning. We called it the duty room of the operations duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And for clarification, that office was next to the stairs on the first level of the building. Right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, like I said, there's the staircase, and then the first room on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And they have a little bed in there, too, where they can rest so they don't have to leave their location at any time. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Used to be a bed in it for a while. I can't remember when exactly. And then the commander had it removed. Certainly there was a table inside, a handful of chairs, a metal cupboard, a TV set, some phones. And for a while, there was a bed, but I think that was early, not towards the end of the war. I think by that time it was gone.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And the switchboard for the brigade headquarters is located up on the third floor, not in the duty officer's room, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The in-house switchboard with two or three people manning it, two a shift, I believe, it was on the last floor, second floor if I'm looking correctly. And down the corridor to the left, the last room on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm just going to ask you to verify the duties of the operational duty officer. He's one to monitor the course of combat operations. Right? And to inform the commander of major changes. He's the information person that relays information to the commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I guess we're just going to go through the same problem as before. But if we are going to do this, she should at least complete the sentence because she left off a key part of that first sentence. So...

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'm not sure what key part Mr. McCloskey is referring to, Your Honour. I'm just using the verbs mainly, to monitor, to inform, to be familiar with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Ms. Sinatra, the way you are introducing the document is a little bit strange to me, at least. Earlier you asked a question to the witness, and if you did not get the answer you need, you may show him a document pointing to certain, you know, discrepancies between the statement, documents, and the testimony of this witness. But it seems to me that you make it the other way around. So I don't know whether it's a good practice or not. If you want to ask some relevant questions, just put it direct to this witness. Then you may show him the documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honour. I thought also that the use of documents was for verification, authentication, by the witness, and I was just having him verify and authenticate that these are the rules that they go by at the Zvornik Brigade headquarters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: These rules are already there, and I believe that it's kind of public, you know, in that brigade, public document in that brigade. So I don't think it's necessary to verify those documents through this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Okay, well I'll ask him a general question about it, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: The operational duty officer at the brigade headquarters cannot issue orders; he can only relay messages and information. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not true. As I said last week, and as the rules clearly state, the work of the operations duty officer has two components, if that's the right expression, it has two distinct elements or two functions if you like. Internal duty, like the duty officer for engineering at brigade level, and as the name itself clearly says, there's the operative function. And what that means is simply command. Therefore, the operations duty officer can, under a certain set of circumstances, on behalf of the commander or deputy commander or on behalf of the operations duty officer of the Drina Corps issue certain orders to the extent that he is authorised to do so. This would be putting it as succinctly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: You said that he could issue orders on behalf of the commander. When you say that he's not really issuing an order, the commander has told him to issue an order, he's just relaying it on, isn't that right? So the order is actually coming from the commander, not the duty officer.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, the operations duty officer specifically of the Zvornik Brigade could issue orders on behalf of the commander and on behalf of the duty officer, operations duty officer of the Drina Corps. I've said this two or three times at least today, the principle of unity of command. The brigade commander is the brigade commander. It can't be 15 different people in the brigade to give orders. Only the commander does. At the same time, this is not a purely mechanic procedure. The remaining people down the chain of command are not merely couriers in relaying these orders. So it was within this framework that we carried out certain activities, and the same applies to the operations duty officer. The commander is responsible for me issuing an order on his behalf also. This does not relieve him of his responsibility. And the same applies to the operations duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: But the operations duty officer doesn't create an order on his own. He has to have been given the mandate by the commander to write an order on his behalf and transfer it somewhere else, doesn't he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At certain critical moments in the commander's absence, then he could issue an order in the spirit of previous plans and ideas. However, he's duty-bound to inform the commander as soon as possible, inform the commander or the operations duty officer of the Drina Corps, or as was most frequently the case, both of these officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Let me ask you about -- it says the duty officer -- operations duty officer must have the instruction for work, the plan for the immediate security and defence of the command post. So for anything he does, there's a plan given to him ahead of time that he has to implement in case of an emergency, like a fire marshal. Is that what that represents?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our operations duty officer, the one we're talking about, there was an order by the command of the Drina Corps envisaging point by point the documents that the operations duty officer was supposed to keep at all times. And we were supposed to follow these instructions closely. Many of those plans had been drawn up. I can't list them all right now. Maybe I could remember a number of those. But still, it's impossible to foresee everything. It was wartime situation. So if your question was that he could do nothing on his own but instead had to consistently apply a previously envisaged plan, then my answer is it is impossible to predict everything. It is impossible to foresee everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: But let me refresh your memory about one of the documents that the operational duty officer was to keep, and the last sentence says: "The handover of duty is recorded in the operations logbook." Doesn't it? And that operations logbook is missing, isn't it, the duty-shift change book?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I've already explained, this duty-shift change book was not among the documents that I handed over to the Office of the Prosecutor. I simply didn't find it. Perhaps because it wasn't there. But that's the long and short of it, that's why I didn't hand it over. This book records the change of shift of the operations duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: In fact, last week in your direct testimony, you listed the documents that the duty officer was responsible for maintaining. I believe they included the logbook, the shift book, and a workbook. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely, also the regular and interim reports included there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And the logbook, shift book, and workbook are documents that had been in your possession for about four years during the investigation of this case, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to other documents, I did have those, too, yes, since spring 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'd like to refer again to your 2002 statement, which is D28/3. And you stated on page -- I guess it's ERN number 10008161.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you have the English?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I just have an ERN number. I'm looking for the page myself. It's 10008161. And Your Honours, I don't find it in here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: But do you remember in your statement saying that as a military expert, you know that the operations duty officer can never become a superior to the battalion commander?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember ever having stated that I was a military expert. I completed a certain degree of military education, and I've detailed this for you. As you said earlier, in all units, there was the position of duty officer. In a battalion, you had the battalion duty officer. In the brigade, we had the operations duty officer. In independent companies, they also had duty officers such as the military police unit you have referred to. So that was the line of communication in terms of duty and duty officers across the units. Now, as to how the operations duty officer related to the brigade commander, much in the same way at his own level, of course, the operations duty officer of a battalion would have related to the commander of that particular battalion. So that's what this refers to.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'd like to go in the 2000 transcript to page 40 in the English version where Krstan Simic clears up your statement by saying "by having the status of duty officer, is he in a superior position or is he just a link between units on the ground and a commander?" And your answer on page 40, line 22 is that "he is not in a superior position, but" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry. My April 2000, I don't have any such thing on page 40. Perhaps I'm looking in the wrong place.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Page 40, line 18, Krstan Simic is talking first.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And then Dragan Obrenovic says: "He is not in a superior position, but he is in a certain position of being a link." And I think Mr. Simic helped you clear that up. And that's pretty much what the duty officer is, is he's a link between command and the rest of the brigade, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're speaking about two different things here. We can't -- if we look in the same way at two different things, then the result would be that there are only five commanders -- that there are as many as five commanders in a unit, in a military unit. The next rule concerning the unity of command, only the brigade commander can be superior to the battalion commander, directly superior. And that's how it was. The operations duty officer, now that's an internal position of duty. And as such, he has certain rights based on his duties. He also has obligations based on these duties. And certainly, the operations duty officer is not superior to the battalion commander. His superior would have been in this specific case the brigade commander. But if you look at the duties, the duties you showed me some time ago, you will see that there are certain moments specified by orders where the operations duty officer can issue orders on behalf of the commander or of the operations duty officer of the unit in charge. Now, whether he goes directly to the commander or through the battalion, that's a different thing. That's what I meant when I said that the operations duty officer was not superior to the battalion commander because the brigade commander would have been.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Is it a duty of the duty officer to know where his commander is at all times?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to go to another subject right now. The capture of prisoners --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it's time for a break.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Okay. Perfect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We could come to another subject after the break. We will resume at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Sinatra, before you start, I think I have to remind you or everybody that we have only one hour left for the morning session. We have to break at 1.30.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. There's a housekeeping issue, too. Interpretation came down and said that in the transcript today marked at 11:52:47, I think, that when I was questioning Mr. Obrenovic about the documents that are the responsibility of the duty officer, he said "logbook, shift book, and workbook." And they didn't get shift book into the interpretation, at 11:52:47.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. But from the English transcript, I see that we have three, logbook, shift book, and workbook.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'm just going by the note she made for me. If it's correct, I don't know if I need to reask the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think the best way is for you to reask this question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Because I don't know if he heard the question at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Shift, logbook was not interpreted into B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: You basically stated in your prior testimony that your responsibilities for recording and reporting of the duty officer, the operation duty officer, was to maintain a logbook, a shift book, and a workbook. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and also daily reports and interim reports as needed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'll have to read it from the transcript. Okay. Thank you. I think we covered that answer. Thank you very much. I'm going to move forward. I would like to bring out what's been marked -- no, never mind. I'm going to another subject now. I wanted to ask you with your knowledge and training in the Geneva Convention that you received in military school, you are aware that the capture of prisoners of war or prisoners during a combat operation is a legitimate military operation, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And the transportation of refugees whose lives might be in danger if they stayed in a combat situation is a legitimate military operation, too, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I now want to move to the engineering equipment available in July 1995. As deputy commander, you're familiar with the equipment that belonged to the engineering company, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it may be said so.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Well, in July of 1995, the engineering company didn't have that much -- not very much heavy equipment that was owned by the engineering company, did they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A little while ago, I provided some explanation about that. The engineers company and the logistics had at their disposal technical equipment from two sources. One source was the fund of the army of Republika Srpska, so this was our ownership. There were lots of lorries. I don't know how many. And a few other machines. I can't remember exactly what they were. Those things were our ownership which we could use at any time, and we could also use equipment from civilian companies in Zvornik in case of mobilisation or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Well, I think you're confusing the equipment that was owned by the Zvornik Brigade with the equipment that could be readily requisitioned from the civilian sector, from the factories that were located there. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to bring out what's been marked for identification purposes as D12/3. It's the Zvornik Brigade Engineering Summary report for 1995. We received this document from Mr. Obrenovic on 27th of September, 2003. Mr. Obrenovic, while you're looking at this document, this is a document that you're very familiar with as being commander of the Zvornik Brigade because this is a report that's written every year by the chief of engineering, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the Zvornik Brigade was Lieutenant-Colonel Vinko Pandurevic. And I specified when I was the one discharging these duties, I also said when I became commander of the 303rd Motorised Brigade. But as the chief of staff and the superior to Jokic, you are right. I knew in rough outlines via these reports what was going on, and these reports were drafted either towards the end of the year or at the beginning of the next year, and then forwarded to whomever it was forwarded to.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And these are what we call standard operating procedure for the brigade, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Truth be told, whether they are standard or not, I don't know. Probably there was some order issued by the corps command, something that was to serve their annual summary. I believe that this was preceded by an order issued by the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here in the heading, the order is actually quoted.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, to be realistic about it, though, in December of 1995, even though you didn't assume the official position of commander of the Zvornik Brigade until 1996, in December you were acting commander of the brigade, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: December? I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: The report basically gives an inventory and a list of the tasks that the engineering department had been engaged in for 1995. Is that what this includes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here the units are itemised.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Engineering fortification work in 1995, data on wounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Legitimate --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May the counsel speak into the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Legitimate operations that the engineering company should be involved in, such as construction of defensive positions, laying mines and defence lines? Now they're involved in the infantry and actually involved in combat operations in 1995. Right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some 15 soldiers from the engineering company participated in the combat on Snagovo. If a unit, some other unit, was to be sent out of the zone of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade, some of the engineering troops were added to those troops, and they then maybe participated in the combat that was taking place in that area. But most of the time, they did their own engineering work.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And part of that engineering work includes using the large equipment to build things such as trenches or barriers between combat fronts, between positions on the front -- of the combat operation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: In fact, that would be fortification of positions. That would include mining, digging trenches, anything that they can do to help strengthen the position of the VRS during a combat operation.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And if you see on number 8, it lists the equipment that was available via the VRS at that time. And according to the list, it's on page 4 under number 8, it says the things that were army contingent that belonged to the VRS. That was a tugboat, a motorboat, eight chainsaws, two Tomos - whatever that is - one mine detector, and three sets of mine-laying and mine-lifting equipment. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And if we --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And if we go to B, we go to much heavier equipment that says it came from the requisitioned fund. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And the requisition fund would be heavy equipment that had been requisitioned by some superior from the civilian division to operate and be used by the engineering department, or by the Zvornik Brigade. It doesn't mean it was necessarily used by the engineering department, though.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it may be said so.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And then we have here: "One bulldozer, TG 140." I don't know -- is that a torpedo? One bulldozer, TG 220. The first one, 12 years old. The second one, 7 years old. One bulldozer, TG 75; 20 years old and broken. One bulldozer, TG 110; 6 years and working. One excavator, a torpedo skip; 15 years, working. One excavator, a BGH 7; 10 years old and working. And two carryall trailers. Is that what it says was the equipment that the engineering department may have had access to, not belonging to the VRS but requisitioned from the civilian portion of Zvornik Municipality?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Truth be told, I'm not clear whether what is listed here under B is just a possibility, what can be requisitioned, or whether this lists the things that had already been requisitioned by that time. I believe that at the moment when this report was being drawn up, that all these things had already been requisitioned. But it may mean both things. This is the way I interpret it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: So what you're saying is that these are things that maybe were available in the civilian community to be requisitioned, but not necessarily requisitioned at that time by the Zvornik Brigade. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is not clear whether this list refers to the things that could be requisitioned at any given moment, or whether this refers to the things that had been requisitioned by the time when this report was drawn up. I am inclined to believe that the second case is true. At the moment, when this report was drafted, all these things had already been in the possession of our unit. But it doesn't transpire clearly from the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you tell me, we have the next list, C, which is war booty. Right? And under war booty, I assume these are pieces of equipment that were seized from the BiH army, either the 2nd Battalion or the 28th Division. Is that right? And I see under the --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't have to mean that. This was seized from the enemy, and we cannot say for a fact from which unit those things were seized.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Okay. But the only units operating in the area was the 2nd Battalion and the 28th Division. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 2nd Corps, and the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you. We have under this list of booty one machine called an excavator King, broken. Do you see that? It's at the bottom of the list of war booty.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Are you familiar with that piece of equipment, the King?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a small excavator, looking like a tractor. It has a spoon in the front, claws in the front, and a claw in the back. I don't know whether I'm using the right terms when I'm describing this piece of equipment. I'm a layperson when it comes to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Well, I just wanted to ask you, again, after the war, you were, in fact, the subject of an investigation while you were commander regarding this King equipment, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. When it came to the King, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: So you're claiming there would be no written reports from Sergeant Savic, the security officer of the Zvornik Brigade, relating to an investigation regarding you and this piece of equipment. Right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what he did. He never showed me any such thing. I know that there was investigation, but not involving this piece of equipment. Whether he ever investigated anything that involved this piece of equipment, I don't know. It is possible, but he never showed it to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: So you're saying you never marked this piece of equipment as broken and sold it on the black market, did you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a prescribed procedure in order to do these things. First of all, a thing had to be written off in case a piece of equipment was broken. The corps command would then sell it. So this is just in short outlines. If you're interested in any more details, be my guest.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: That's the standard procedure for this. But this piece of King equipment was the subject of an investigation that did not follow standard procedure for used or broken equipment, did it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know any of the details. Savic never informed me about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: After the investigation was halted by General Andric, isn't it true that you tried to have Sergeant Savic removed as security officer of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was just the other way around. The security officers -- actually, I tried to place the security officers under Savic's control. I wanted to implement the things that Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic had wanted at one point. I didn't succeed, and then they came up with things like this King and other things, but they never informed me about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: During July 1995 and August 1995, was it really you and Major Galic that requisitioned the earth-moving equipment from the civilian companies, from Glinica, the aluminum company, and from Novi Izvor, the brick-making company?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Galic, are you referring to this person who is in jail here in the Detention Unit, this Galic?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: My correction, it's Major Galic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that what you're saying is correct. Not only that I don't think that, but I am absolutely sure that this is not correct. On the 14th, I was in Snagovo, as you already know. And if my memory serves me well, Major Galic replaced the forward command post, Drago Nikolic. And two or three days ago, we saw a handwritten note written by him from the forward command post. I don't know whether he was in the position to requisition anything at that time. As far as I know, he was at the forward command post at the time. And I myself was on Snagovo, so I also did not requisition any equipment. In any case, it is not the chief of staff who is in the position to do the requisitioning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: During that time you were deputy commander, weren't you, or commander, acting commander?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 14th, I was deputy commander. This was my role at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Obrenovic. The requisition process is a really strict process in order to requisition civilian equipment, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a very strict procedure, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And doesn't the requisition have to come through the Ministry of Defence for approval?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, if you stick to the rules, then the procedure is prescribed very accurately, what you do. And if you abide by the rules, you must go to the Ministry of Defence, or rather, one of its local departments in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: The chief of engineering could never directly requisition anything from the civilian companies, could he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a rule, no. In practice, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: You mean he could requisition items from the civilian companies? I mean, has there ever been any moment where you saw an order from the chief of engineering to requisition equipment from the brick-laying company or the aluminum company?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see any such order. I have seen requests, not as to the 14th. But the period before and after that, engineers would write a request signed by Jokic or another of their commanders over there, depending who was there at the time. They would sometimes forward this to Galic, or rather the personnel department. And sometimes they would go directly to the Ministry of Defence and sometimes directly to the factory itself. They're probably best placed to tell you about this, the engineers over there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Okay. You're probably right. But the chief of engineer definitely doesn't have the authority under any rule to requisition equipment from the civilian population, does he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Strictly speaking, under the rules, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to move on to another subject. You are aware that there were several meetings held at the Zvornik Brigade headquarters while you were acting commander to organise the testimony that everybody was going to present to the Office of the Prosecutor who had just sent invitations to members of the Zvornik Brigade. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard of these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: You never participated in any of the meetings?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not official meetings. I'm not sure if when you say "meeting," you mean for example when I met Major Jokic showing him parts of the workbook? Maybe it's possible for you to refer to something like that as a meeting. There are many such occasions, but if you have in mind an official occasion, more official occasion as in meeting an official...

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I have more in mind an official meeting that was called by either Miletic or Andric from the main staff organisation to -- and the Drina Corps to organise and talk to all of the potential witnesses that had been called by the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not attend the meeting organised by General Andric or General Miletic. I was at the time in Belgrade in school. Had I been in Zvornik at the time, I probably would have attended the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And this was in 1999 you were in Belgrade in school, fall?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This additional education began in early 1998 and went on throughout 1999, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: So then you weren't fighting on the front -- okay, I can see in 1999. But in 1999, you didn't attend the meeting, and you didn't attend the meeting that was arranged in 2000 either. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you that I did not attend the meeting chaired by General Miletic or that chaired by General Andric. I attended a number of meetings with General Andric because he was our commander. Now, specifically.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Specifically, during your interview with the OTP in April of 2000, you were represented by an attorney named Krstan Simic from Banja Luka, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And you also know that Mr. Simic represented Mr. Jokic in December of 1999 and in April of 2002. You know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And you knew that at the time, in 1999 and 2000?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that in 1999. But I did in 2000.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And, in fact, Mr. Simic not only represented you and Mr. Jokic, but he also represented Mr. Jevtic, who was commander of the engineering department, right, engineering company? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jevtic was indeed the commander of the engineering company. And he was represented by him. Mr. Krstan Simic also represented Ms. Plavsic, as far as I remember. He represented everyone. At the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska, Mr. Krstan Simic was recommended to me as counsel, but I had never even heard of him up to that point. It was their choice really.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: He was not the Ministry of Defence for the Republic of Srpska in 1999 and 2000. That's something that has happened since those dates, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean Mr. Simic, Krstan Simic?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Mr. Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must apologise. I never said that he was the Ministry of Defence for the Republic of Srpska. What I wanted to say - and maybe I did not express myself too clearly - the summons was handed to me via the Ministry of Defence. And when I was physically there at the Ministry of Defence to consult about these issues being an active officer, as I was, issues regarding my potential counsel, they, the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska, told me, or rather advised me that Mr. Krstan Simic had been appointed as my counsel, and mine and also appointed to represent everyone else. So that's how I found, how I came across Krstan Simic because I had not known him before.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Right. And these meetings that were held --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we go too much deeply into counsel and choice of counsel, if we could have some statement of the relevancy. This is a rather sensitive and important topic, the right to counsel. And if there is some relevance, I have no objection. But at this point, there is no relevance established, and I don't see the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Ms. Sinatra, what's your case? What's your position on that?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The relevance is that because they were all assigned Krstan Simic, with conflicts of interest between all the parties, then they effectively did not have the right to choose counsel. This is all part of the motion to express the statements which -- if you want to go into private session for this line of questioning, I would be happy to. But I do have a lot of questions about Mr. Simic, and then I have questions about someone else that the Prosecution has asked me to go into private session about. So if you want to take this whole line of questioning in private session, I do not object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Mr. Simic told you what Mr. Jokic has said in his 1999 interview, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, for the most part not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: "For the most part not"?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, not. Maybe, you know, in two or three sentences, three at most.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: When you went to have your interview with the OTP in Banja Luka, you and Dragan Jevtic rode together for the interviews, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The interview on the 2nd of April, 2000 -- no, I did not ride together with Dragan Jevtic. Rather, I went there with my brother. Mr. Jokic was interviewed the day before. I can't remember when Jevtic was interviewed, but I did go together with Jevtic to Banja Luka, but that was on a later occasion, not when the interviews took place. If I remember correctly, I reached Banja Luka on the 1st of April in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And you met with your attorney at that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We met in a cafe on the 1st, in the evening. It was night actually already. He came together with Dragan Jokic. We sat in a cafe, and the two of them came along.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And then you're saying that Dragan Jevtic did not ride with you to the interview on the following day?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 2nd, we had -- that's, I had my interview in Trnje [phoen], near Banja Luka. And I rode there on my own, certainly not with Jevtic. I remember that I did ride to Banja Luka with Jevtic, but that was at a later date. That was later. That was not for the interview that took place on the 1st, or rather 2nd of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: So if Jevtic said that he rode with you to the interview, he would be mistaken. Right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The interview, as long as we're talking about the interview which took place on the 2nd of April, 2000, to the best of my recollection, I rode accompanied by my brother. And we set out on the 1st of April in the afternoon hours. I don't think Jevtic was with me then. To the best of my recollection, I did ride with Jevtic to Banja Luka, but that was later. And that was not for the interview.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to distribute to the witness now what has been marked as D2/3a and b for identification purposes. And there's a B/C/S version and an English version, with the assistance of Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Mr. Obrenovic, have you seen this document before? I'm showing you what's marked D2/3a and b for identification purposes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember having seen this. I may have, but I really can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: So this is a letter from the Republic of Srpska Ministry of Defence dated June 26th, 2000. And it's written on your behalf, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, my name is there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: So you're saying that the government didn't copy you on a letter that they were writing on your behalf?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was not written on my behalf. In the header you can see "Republika Srpska Ministry of Defence." But the document was drafted by someone on behalf of the minister of defence. In item 1, in addition to other six names, you can see my name. But I'm telling you I don't recall that. I may have received this, but frankly I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And the subject of why you're mentioned in the letter is because of the OTP rescheduling your interview. Right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, the first interview was supposed to take place in March, rather, in early March 2000. The gentlemen from the Office of the Prosecutor were not there. Then I came back on the 2nd of April. I was interviewed. And this is a document from June. In August, there was a further interview.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Well, when you had your interview on 2nd of April, 2000, it ended with that you were going to be interviewed again at a future date. And so this is rescheduling your future date interview, isn't it? Because it says that these people have not received summons yet.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was sometime in August, the second interview. It may have been the 19th of August, but I am certain, however, that it was in August.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: This letter was written between your first interview and your second interview, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And as commander of the Zvornik Brigade, you didn't receive a copy of it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I don't remember. I may have. I may not have. A summons for an interview with a number of documents enclosed, yes, I did get those. Now, whether I got this particular document as part of that attachment, I don't know. There was a summons. There was some sort of an explanation that we would not be arrested during the 24 hours preceding and after the interview. There was a bundle of documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And this one is signed by the minister Manojlo Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And you were aware that the Republika Srpska was not happy with the techniques used by the Prosecutor to interview witnesses from the Republic of Srpska?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to be quite honest, I was not familiar with some of the details because they didn't tell us. My impression, though, was that at the time, there was some form of silent pressure, tacit pressure, applied for as few people to end up going. That's -- that was my impression. What they told us was it's down to you. It's your decision. But then, next, next thing we knew, they would tell us, you'd better not go. Those who end up going are finished and done for. But the decisions that were taken at the level of government, I really can't say. I really can't speak about that. And the same thing goes for the main staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Well, I think you're talking about coercive tactics or pressure put on potential suspects by the VRS. This letter, from your minister, is talking about improper techniques used by the Prosecutor when interviewing witnesses. Are you familiar -- have you heard that there was complaints from the witnesses that the OTP was pressuring them during their interviews?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard no such thing. Later, after my second -- after my interview on the 2nd of April, when I talked to my superior officers, they made remarks along the lines of why I, myself, or rather Mr. Krstan had allowed for the interview to go for that long, and that it should have been interrupted and done in two or three days. This is information that reached me eventually. As for the other things that may have been discussed, I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Let me ask you if since this letter was written between your first and your second interview, if there were changes in the interviewing techniques based upon this letter. According to their allegations during interviews, human dignity and spiritual integrity are being insulted. "Interviews are exhausting, up to 12 hours in duration. Threats of arrest are incessantly resorted to. It is impossible to consume food. And in general, there is a humiliating treatment on the part of the investigators. In regard to this, and in accordance with Articles 12, 13, and 14 of the RS constitution, Articles 5, 6, and 10 of general declaration on human rights, as well as with Resolution 217A (iii) of General Assembly dating from 1 December 1948, we demand that you inform the Prosecutor's Office of The Hague Tribunal about this so that a fair and correct treatment during interviews would be provided. "We also deem it necessary that the interviewed persons should be enabled to read and sign the minutes of the interviews, or provided with tape recordings of the interviews. We also demand that you provide through the Office of the Tribunal the defrayal of costs of interviewed persons." And it's signed the minister. Based on this letter that was written on behalf of all of the persons who were being interviewed by the OTP at that time, and based on the fact that you are one of the citizens of the Republic of Srpska, did you see a difference between the technique of interviewing you on the 2nd April versus August 2000?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, none whatsoever. The interview may have even taken place in the same room, and everything was the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: So it was the same technique?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was just a room with two desks, a small tape recorder. So the interview was audiorecorded. No pictures were taken. But you have minutes of all that. I can find this in our transcripts. In my case, that was the case. At the end, we were paid expenses, the first time and the second time. I was given two fruit juices at a time. I didn't drink coffee. I also was given sandwich during the interview. And it was the same the first time and the second time. As far as I'm concerned, the situation was very similar on both occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It's time for a break. And we'll resume at 3.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.37 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Sinatra, shall we continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. But I'd like to put something on the record in private session for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Sorry, I can't get the microphone closer. Hello, Mr. Obrenovic. I hope you had a nice lunch break.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Yes, thank you, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Before the Zvornik Brigade headquarters were searched, the ICTY or the SFOR sent SFOR -- the commissioner of the high representative or whatever, sent a memo to the Ministry of Defence asking permission to search the Zvornik Brigade headquarters, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The high representative of the United Nations, SFOR, and the ICTY are three very distinct organisations. Form of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra, please rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Before the Zvornik Brigade headquarters were searched, a notice was sent to the Ministry of Defence by members of SFOR, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't work in the Ministry of Defence, so I really don't know what they were sent. I saw the investigators, including Mr. McCloskey, on that first morning when they arrived. Perhaps the ministry did receive some notice, but the Zvornik Brigade didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: But the search was conducted in coordination of SFOR forces and evidently of the Office of the Prosecutor. Right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the morning of the 6th of March, 1998, a group of people turned up, perhaps 10 to 15 of them, I don't really remember. There were several senior officers from SFOR, and the rest were wearing civilian clothes. And Mr. McCloskey was among them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could have a statement of relevant or foundation for this. If this is a challenge to the search warrant or a motion to not have the material admissible, I think it's a little late. Otherwise, the relevancy of this line of question, if we could at least have some idea of where we're going.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll be happy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It is very clear to me, at least, because the Defence counsel made some allegations concerning the custody of the documents, as well as the chain of the custody of the documents. I believe this is the beginning. Let's begin from here to see how far that we could go. You may proceed, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I just wanted to make sure that I'm clear on this. These documents have not been admitted into evidence as yet. They are simply submitted by the Prosecutor at this point, so their admissibility is still at question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: The searches of the Zvornik Brigade headquarters were granted by M. Milovanovic and Jokic, the minister, weren't they? And he's the same person that signed the other document, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about those details. When I was told what it was about, I spoke over the phone with the corps command. And after some time had passed, they sent me to talk to a general in the general staff. And I did talk to him. This might have been roughly speaking half an hour later, one of those generals conveyed a message to me. He said everything was all right, and that I should allow the search to go ahead. As you said, the offices and the documents in the building. And they gave me certain instructions as to how this should be organised. What he got from the ministry, I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Okay. But you, as commander of the Zvornik Brigade, were informed about the impending search of the premises three days before the search actually occurred, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: So how many days were you informed before the search occurred?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That morning, when they arrived at the entrance. I said that a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: So it's your testimony today that you had no advance notice that the search was going to occur at the Zvornik Brigade headquarters?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In specific terms, nobody ordered me anything along those lines. I did know that a search had been conducted in Banja Luka on some premises, army premises there. But I was able to see that from the information media. But I really don't remember anybody having ordered me to do anything. And I saw on the news bulletin just like everything else that sometime prior to that period, they had searched some premises in Banja Luka. And that's all I knew.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: So we're not talking about a direct order. But you found out informally that the Zvornik Brigade headquarters was going to be searched ahead of time, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't say that. I learned about it, like everybody else, from the information media that a search had been conducted on the premises of one of the commands in Banja Luka. I didn't mention the Zvornik Brigade at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: So when you found the search was taking place in Banja Luka, you then went through the Zvornik Brigade headquarters and took all of the documents and materials that might be relevant to your Defence or to what happened in Zvornik Brigade headquarters? You took them, and you deposited them with General Miletic, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: General Miletic came to the Zvornik Brigade and took the documents, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Okay. Let's talk about Mr. Jokic's quest for these documents. You know that all through these proceedings, requests for disclosure of the documents from the Zvornik Brigade have been made by Defence counsel. Right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: The documents --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't know what the factual basis of that question was, but the material from the Zvornik Brigade was provided in a searchable CD years ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No, no, I think the Defence counsel is not talking about the documents disclosed by the OTP, but the documents in the custody of Mr. Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If that's the case, Your Honour, there has been no request whatsoever that I can recall that she is talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In a historical context, very recently when we found out about it, yes, those were delivered. But she is going back into some sort of bizarre historical context that does not exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Sinatra, I understand that there's a point in your question. But you have to put it in a proper form.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Well, I will just let the historical public documents of this case, starting from the request for disclosure of materials under Rule 68, and disclosure of all documents, including the duty officer's book, the duty logbooks, which have been requested long -- at least a year ago in this case. And it's reflected in the public record of this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But that's a different matter. Right?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Because the OTP just got those documents before the trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: May I proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Mr. Obrenovic, you have been in custody at the UN Detention Centre for how long?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the 15th of April, 2001.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And you had custody of some documents from the Zvornik Brigade from 1999 until 2003, June, when you decided to disclose them. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And all the documents that you disclosed to the OTP after pleading guilty, plus the documents that you just disclosed on September 26th of 2003, have been in your custody during that four-year period. Right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: In fact, I want to go through exactly what happened to the documents that we're talking about. You picked up the documents in the spring of 1999 in Mali Zvornik, which is Serbia, before the NATO bombing campaign, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And these documents were taken from the Mali Zvornik military storage warehouse located there, and it's a VRS warehouse located across the river in Serbia. Isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are facilities -- actually, it's not a warehouse belonging to the army of Republika Srpska. It was a barracks belonging to the Yugoslav army. And in one of the rooms, they stored not only the documents you mentioned, but many others as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: But it wasn't in Republic of Srpska; it was outside of the Republic of Srpska in what is now Serbia and Montenegro. Right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And you collected these documents on two separate occasions with the assistance of General Miletic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without the assistance of General Miletic on two occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Well, you had gone to Mali Zvornik, and you met with General Miletic. You discussed the documents; he showed you the documents. And then you went home and thought about it for a little while. Right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not how it was. I can explain what actually happened. I have already explained once. If need be, I'm ready to explain again.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Obrenovic, you have explained it once to the Office of the Prosecutor. But the Trial Chamber has never heard this explanation, so that's why we're doing it again. So actually, you went to Mali Zvornik on two separate occasions. And along with General Miletic, you selected documents, and he copied documents. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not true.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Okay. Well, tell me what happened, then. How did you get those documents from Mali Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is how it was: In the barracks in Mali Zvornik, I had two meetings with General Miletic. And as I've already explained, following orders from the corps commander, General Andric, I went to the barracks at Mali Zvornik, and I didn't know who there was at all. So that I could ensure for the man working there - I didn't who it was - to supply him with accommodation and food. When I went to the barracks in the afternoon, I came across General Miletic there with two other men I didn't know and they were looking through something, some documents. And they were copying some as well. I went up to him to tell him where my assignment was, and told him where he would find accommodation and food. And we sat down and had a cup of coffee, and sat to the side of the room, and I didn't have an opportunity, nor did he offer to do so, nor did I ask him whether I could look at any of the documents at all. That was one of my meetings with General Miletic. After a short space of time, I left. And perhaps several days later, let's say two or three, I turned up once again in the afternoon to see whether the general had any comments to make about his accommodation or anything of that sort. We had a brief conversation, an informal one, and once again, I didn't look at any documents. He didn't offer any documents to me, nor did I ask to see any. So during those two meetings, I did see that there were some documents there. To be quite frank, I found it rather strange. And as you said, that gave me the idea after giving it some thought that it would be a good idea if I saw what was there, because nobody told me about it, nor did I know anything about what was there. So after some time, I tried to get to the same room. General Miletic was there for five or six days. I don't know exactly how long, perhaps seven. And then he left. After some time had gone by, I went to try and look through those documents myself, alone. But I didn't succeed in doing so because the guards on duty there didn't let me pass without written permission from the corps commander. I phoned him up and asked him whether he would give the okay for me to do that. And he said yes, he would. And I received two written permits or letters of permission that he, the corps commander, was granting permission for me to be able to go and take a look at -- or rather, he gave permission for access to those premises. So on two occasions during the day, I took advantage of that opportunity. I gave them my permit. I was allowed to pass, and I went there twice. So that was my third and fourth arrival there. I was alone on this occasion. Miletic wasn't there, and Miletic didn't, in fact, know, unless he was told by General Andric that I had been granted permission and had gone through the documents on that subsequent occasion. So the first two times, I was able to access the premises with the permit that I was given. I went through the documents. There were piles of documents.
