And the ones I managed to secure are the ones that I passed over to the Prosecutor, to the OTP. That is in general terms what happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Okay. So General Miletic was there on his own copying and searching mission in Serbia with the documents that were stored there in one room as part of the JNA. Right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Miletic was there with two other individuals. On both occasions when I went there, he was there with two other men.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And then you went back with your permission slip from General Andric to look at the documents that were stored in Serbia and Montenegro. Right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This might have been some ten days later. General Miletic had finished what he was doing, and after some time had elapsed, I managed to get the permission slip from Andric. And then I was able to go there on my own.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: You were aware that these were documents that the people from the SFOR search were really looking for, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know what they did there. There were documents from various brigades, from the Drina Corps, some documents about the Drina Corps. So by and large, there was part of the archives there from the whole mass of documents that I've just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Stored in another country, separate from the Republic of Srpska. Right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Now, you took the original documents after two days of searching from Mali Zvornik, and you took them back to your home in Zvornik, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and there weren't two days of searching. I just spent several hours there at a time. I didn't spent the whole day there because I thought I'd be able to return and go through them again. So perhaps several hours each day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: But my question was you took the documents with you back to Zvornik, across the border, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I took them to my apartment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And then you kept them at your apartment for about a month, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And then you said you taped the box up. And after a month --

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we may need to go into private session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Obrenovic, the ones that you didn't turn over in June of 2003 included Zvornik Brigade documents that you knew were relevant to Mr. Jokic's defence. Right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've explained how the selection was made. I never stopped to think about any sort of relevance. I was looking at my agreement with the OTP, which spoke about all sorts of cooperation regarding Srebrenica and the time defined in that agreement. And that's how I turned over documents in the first batch.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Now, on June 3rd, 2003, when these documents first surfaced, the Prosecutor did ask you if this was all of the documents, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And you replied "yes, these are all the documents"?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And the ones you just turned over on 26 of September, 2003, the Prosecutor just asked you "now, are these all the documents." Right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I handed over everything that I had up to then. I have nothing else with me. I handed over everything, even those which according to my estimate were relevant to my agreement, everything that had been taken from Mali Zvornik. If you look at the contents of these documents, some of this has nothing whatsoever to do with the time when things happened or the place when things happened. Some of them are relevant, some of them aren't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Some of them are relevant. But the truth is, the Prosecutor asked you after you pled guilty and it entered into their agreement to tell the truth. They said on June 3rd are these all of the documents, and you said "yes," didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I explained why.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And that was after your agreement to fully cooperate. Isn't that true? And in fact, you didn't tell the truth on June 3rd, 2003, did you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I misunderstood my obligations. And hence, my mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And you may not have told the truth on the 26th of September when you said these are all the documents. Right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that those where will all the documents because there's no reason for me to either hide them or to keep them for something else.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: But we are still missing the Zvornik Brigade duty officer's shift book for July, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is missing because I never found it there. If I had found it, it would have made part of the first group of documents because it would be obvious that the dates indicated in my agreement with the OTP would be mentioned in it. However, I didn't find it in Mali Zvornik; it was never in my position. That's why I could not hand it over.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: But again, you did tell the Prosecutor that you didn't have any more documents in your possession on June 3rd, 2003, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Ms. Sinatra, this is the third time you asked the same question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Mr. Obrenovic, when are you going to turn over all the documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is the point where it is argumentative on argumentative. She has made the point. The witness has answered. It's all very clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I agree with you. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'm going to go to another topic. I would like to bring out the IKM duty officer's logbook, and that is marked P118, I believe. Well, if you don't have a complete version of it to give the witness... These have already been marked for identification as P118, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this logbook?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw a copy of this within the documents that I turned over to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And which time did you turn this over to the Prosecutor? Was it in June or the end of September?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not me who turned over to the Prosecutor. It was the other way around. It was the Prosecutor who turned over these documents to us on CDs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Okay. My mistake. This is for identification purposes, it's P118. It's the forward command post operations duty logbook. And I don't know if I can bring to your attention in that copy, but can you go to 15 July 1995. Okay -- well, we can't -- are you familiar with the logbook? Did you see who filled out the summaries on July 15th, 1995? Was it Major Galic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. If this is what it says here, then I suppose it was. I can look at the handwriting. I'm sure I would be able to recognise it because he has very characteristic handwriting. If I were to be shown this handwriting, then I could be more precise in my answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Well, we'll have to pass that one. I'm trying to move on quickly. I would like to bring out what's been marked as P137a. I think it's the Zvornik Brigade duty officer's logbook. P137a. I know you've seen this document before. You saw it during your direct testimony. It has 11th July, 1995, doesn't it? And then it has 12 July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Summarised and signed by Milan Maric. And then 13th and 14th are missing, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And then it goes to the 15th of July, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there are a few entries made on the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And they are all signed by Drago Nikolic, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It seems like his signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And it's confirmed by Drago Nikolic. Right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Well, the signature's column is where they sign. But isn't it supposed to be an independent person that confirms it under "remarks"?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person who wrote this should have signed it. This looks to me like Lieutenant Nikolic's signature. He was the security officer, the Second-Lieutenant Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to ask you. He was chief of security for the Zvornik Brigade, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And he signed as duty officer on the 15th. Right? And that's his writing on the 15th in the summaries?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: You know that on the 15th of July, Nenad Simic was the duty officer, not Drago Nikolic, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was supposed to be the duty officer. Maybe he even was for a while. Maybe he was later on replaced by Nikolic. But as I've already said, around 1300 hours, I left the command. The commander stayed on. I went to Baljkovice. Now what happened later in the headquarters, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: You saw Nenad Simic on the morning of the 15th as duty officer, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. When I first arrived, the duty officer was Dragan Jokic. That was in the morning. When I arrived, he was still there, and his last entry in the notebook was made at 11.30. That was the entry made by Major Jokic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Well, there's no writing, no handwriting and no signature, by Nenad Simic for the 15th, is there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in this here, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Since we have --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this log, we have what we see.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Well, we have the 13th of July missing, and that should have had Sreten Milosevic's summary and signature, shouldn't it? Because he was the duty officer for the 13th, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it should be.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it isn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And on the 14th, you should have the handwriting and signature of -- summaries and signature of Dragan Jokic because he was the duty officer on the 14th. Right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. He should have entered that. Why he didn't, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: But it isn't there, is it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And the 15th should have Nenad Simic's summaries and signatures, because he was the duty officer on the 15th. But there's no signature or handwriting of Nenad Simic, is there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There should have been Simic's, and if Nikolic replaced him, then there should have been Nikolic's, too. As I said, I didn't remain at headquarters. Perhaps Nenad Simic was attending various funerals. I don't know what it says in his statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And of course you know the standard procedure would be that the commander would be signing a duty shift book each time this took place, but that's missing, too, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a rule, yes, he should sign it if he's there, but what happens fairly often is that the commander isn't there, that I'm not there either. And that we had to do some reporting so that the duty officers replaced themselves to cover each other's shifts themselves. It was wartime, you know, and that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: My question is the shift book is missing. Right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the shift book, duty shift book of the operations duty officer is missing, yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to go to -- just a moment. May I have one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Sinatra, turn off your mic, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the record, we were missing the 15th in the IKM command headquarters forward command logbook. And just for the record, I'd like to go ahead and introduce these documents. They are -- they were missing, but if I could hand them to Mr. Obrenovic, we can identify them by the ERN number. And I could ask about him whether he recognises Major Galic's handwriting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you. Those are missing from the original. Thank you. Okay. Thank you. I've already taken care of the engineering company logbook. I'm sorry, Your Honour. I'm a little -- I'm trying to wrap this up as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Okay. I want to go to the communications capabilities of the VRS. The VRS and the JNA had very sophisticated intercept equipment, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said, I'm a tankist, not a communications man, signalsman. But I do know something about communications and signals. They did have some sort of equipment. Now, if you're asking me as a layman, then my view is that they didn't have any good equipment because all the equipment dated back to the 1960s, and the most recent was 1980. So in electrical engineering, any equipment which is 15 years old would not be state of the art. It would be out of date, so that we used what we had, mostly taken over from the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Right. But by contrast to the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, their equipment was very rudimentary compared to the equipment that belonged to the JNA and belonged to the VRS at the time. Right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, my knowledge as to what the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had was from what I read in the papers and what Vukotic told me. And according to what Vukotic said, I do know that the Srebrenica division had links with the other corps with an S package, which was a very modern device which we did not have. But as I say, all my knowledge on the subject is very superficial.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: But you do know that you had a communications centre right above the Zvornik Brigade headquarters that was stationary, that could receive and send signals under most any circumstances. Right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we had a communications centre up on the hill. I've forgotten what that mount or hill is called now. It was to the northwest of this building, these headquarters. Above Zvornik. There was a container there with some equipment, and three soldiers manned it. It was a stationary communications centre for us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: For the Trial Chamber's information, a tactical intercept versus a regular intercept means that a tactical intercept is some soldier right there on the front climbing on his belly dodging bullets while he's carrying his radio. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how this was organised in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Radio reconnaissance and counter-reconnaissance and intelligence. We organised it at the brigade level by having an intercept centre at Gucevo, and we were able to tap in for the needs of the Zvornik Brigade to the ultrasound and VV bands. And the Drina Corps had a fourth radio reconnaissance device with three intercept stationed, but they were under the command of the Drina Corps. That's how it was where we were. Now what the opposite side, the enemy side had, I really can't say. I saw from the papers given us what was in there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'm sorry. And the JNA had their locations, stationary locations right there, maybe not even 3 kilometres from your locations in Zvornik, across the river, where they had very sophisticated equipment to gather -- intercept information, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear of it. Our intercept group was up at Gucevo where the JNA, or rather at that time in 1995, it was the army of Yugoslavia, no longer the JNA, where they had their intercept groups. And as chief of staff at my level, I didn't another where the army of Yugoslavia had its intercept groups. If it did some 3 kilometres away, I don't know. So I don't know what equipment they had. All I know is that they were under an embargo.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Well, let's just go back to the VRS equipment. You have never seen or heard any of the VRS intercepts that took place on July 13th, 14th, and 15th of 1995, have you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat that. I didn't follow your question. I never saw or heard what?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Let's go back. The only intercepts that you've seen provided by the OTP were intercepts from the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I saw during those days, that is to say, when I returned on the 19th probably, I saw some of those intercepts, intercepted by our 4th radio reconnaissance platoon from Vlasenica. They would send it to us on a piece of paper, like a telegram. It was encoded. And that's what I saw. And later on, Captain Vukotic would show me excerpts from some of those intercepts. Not too often. The intercepts taped by the radio reconnaissance platoon of the 4th Corps because there was one from the Eastern Bosnian Corps, and they would send us something from time to time. So that's what I saw. But our men at Gucevo wouldn't write it down that often. They would ring us up and give us the information by phone.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you for that information because we have been trying to request and get hold of the VRS intercept information from that period of time, and now it's nice to know that it exists. Thank you very much. Now, on the night of the 13th and 14th, you did state that the airwaves were very crowded, and it was very difficult to receive any communication that evening. Right? Especially on the 14th.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I said anything about that, then that referred to the radio devices that I had, the RUP 12, R-U-P 12. And there were about ten of us up at that ambush there, the different commanders, komandir. And some of them were higher officers, but many of them were not trained. So yes, you could say you're right because it was rather crowded, the airwaves.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And I believe you said on page 36 of your debriefing that "it can take -- such a situation can occur in the corps, most important officers of the corps come, and even more likely someone of the main staff, officers of the main staff, to come to a unit and to issue an order without any kind of explanation, especially if he was accompanied by someone from the corps command. The unit should report to the commander when they find the time, but in principle, it doesn't have to ask for the person who came from the superior command. It's not obliged to give any explanation for data protection. The main staff officer can prevent any communications with the brigade, the commanders, and/or the duty officer." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I want to ask you about the procedure for encrypted messages. An encrypted message is one that goes by what we know as telegraph, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, I'm not a communications man. But by the way, let me tell you this: This is a device which was called a teleprinter device encoded. Perhaps it was the M63. It was a code teleprinter device. I'm not sure what the numbers were. It is an electromechanical device which does the encoding via the perforated paper tapes or bands. And that was connected to the radio relay device, north 800. And it used the same bands that the Muslims intercepted, that they used to intercept all our conversations. However, it didn't convey the open text, but like a telegraph, roughly. I'm not sure that my explanations are that precise. But yes, it sent outline radio signals, and the same device would scramble this and turn it back to the original text. That was, if I understand it correctly, what the encoding was like using the teleprinter station up there on the third floor of this building. There were three men there who were especially trained for the job, and that's what they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: So one of those little Motorolas that you communicated with couldn't accept encrypted messages, could it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And the duty officer didn't have any way to send encrypted messages from his office, did he? Only from upstairs.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Everything that was sent out coded had to be written down. So you would have to write using your own hand or computer or typewriter. You could -- you had to have written it down, and then they would encode it and send it on further. It couldn't encode speech the way we're talking now. We didn't have a device that could do that anyway at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Let me ask you, if you remember: The 2nd Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade, they didn't have any way of receiving encrypted messages, did they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. Everything that other people did and that I did at Snagovo is that we used documents for secret commanding of troops. I think that's what it was referred to. And it was a table of signals and an encoded card. Briefly speaking we would prepare reserve frequencies, and then keep moving, shifting frequencies. Or we would state that certain parts on the map would not be Snagovo, but we would be referred to as 61, for example, or something similar. There was another document that was called the conversation book, and this would record the most frequent sentences which would have numbers, sentences given the equivalent of numbers. This was fairly complicated. And when combat started, nobody adhered to any of these things much. And there were few well-trained people. That's why there were so many intercepted conversations, in fact. But otherwise, my answer to your question, once again, the 2nd Battalion did not have any special device. It didn't have an encryption teleprinter station. Only the brigade headquarters had that kind of machinery.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you. And you already said that Zvornik is in a valley, and so you had to have your communication system put up on the mountain so that you could have communications with the rest of the Drina Corps. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only with the Drina Corps, but with anybody else, with our battalions, too. That would go via that radio communication system as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And there was a communication plan that was made each week that would give call names or signals or how you were going to communicate. And it was changed each week by Miroslav Petrovic. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this was every ten days, a month was divided into three parts, from 1 to 10, et cetera. And with Petrovic, yes, we did make plans, communication plans at the brigade with the subordinate units. But with the brigade commander and the corps, we received a communications plan from the communications man in the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: So the call names and everything were devised by the Drina Corps communications person that gives you a plan for a ten-day period?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for communications between the corps command and brigade command. So they devise this concept of Zlatar, Palma, Badem, and all the other code names, call signs that we mentioned. But Miroslav, or rather our communications man devised a communication plan for the brigade command up to the battalions, all for a given assignment such as my own at Snagovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Now, the brigade command, Zvornik Brigade, under exceptional, extraordinary circumstances like occurred on the 13th and 14th, those call names are subject to change depending on the circumstances and what information reconnaissance has found out has leaked. Is that right? That wasn't very clear, but I hope you understand it.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The call names or signs were given to us with the plan, and we would shift frequencies more often.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Those call names having to do with the Drina Corps, locally within the Zvornik Brigade, within a company or a platoon, if there were leaks or problems that occurred, those call names could change within your small zone of communication, couldn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I just explain. We had a communications plan, and an organisations plan from the corps command to the brigade command. So the Drina Corps, the, Zvornik, Bratunac, Sejkovici, Rogisa and all other brigades. So that was one system of communication. Independently of that the other communication system was between the headquarters of the Zvornik Brigade and each of its battalions, 11 battalions and the 4 others. So each battalion had a communications line and had another plan going towards its companies on different frequencies. Now, if something were to leak out, then the name would be changed, each of these people at their own level would change the names. In our brigade, I remember well the names, call names, were changed every ten days. I might be wrong, but I think it was every ten days, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: In combat, if reconnaissance found out there was a leak, you could change it, depending on the circumstances of the emergency. Right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, during combat, what we were able to do was to move to a different frequency. Perhaps during a lull, a new communications plan would be devised. Otherwise, there would be confusion. If someone changed, others didn't. We would usually move to a different channel. And during a lull in the fighting when we could get together, we would reorganise and change. But yes, such situations did occur.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And very rarely were complete conversations intercepted by the BiH army because of this constant changing frequency. Right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from this series of intercepted conversations, we can see that they were quite successful in what they were doing. Sometimes they recorded part of a conversation; at other times, a whole one, depending on the situation. But obviously, at higher levels, they recorded and taped everything. At lower levels, they intercepted only part of the conversations.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: A tactical intercept would be less likely to be complete than an intercept from a communications system -- I mean communications centre. Right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to have about 45 more minutes of questioning that's going into a new subject. If I could just ask for the Court's indulgence to give me a few moments in the morning, I would be able to wrap this up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: How about 30 minutes tomorrow morning?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I will go home and try to work on direct questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. So I give you 30 minutes tomorrow morning because tomorrow, we will have the redirect by the Prosecution, the Judges' questions. And after that, the parties are allowed to ask some questions arising from Judges' questions. Then we'll have the admission of the evidence. And by the way, I asked the parties to submit me with a new list of the documents, because almost every day I got an updated list. At this moment, I am myself confused with those lists. So I want the parties to submit a list of the documents they are going to tender through this witness. So having said that, we are adjourned until tomorrow morning, at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: 4.27 p.m., to be reconvened on Friday, the 10th day of October, 2003, at 9.00 a.m.
